name: McKinsey
summary: McKinsey's interviews are known for two parts: case interviews, where you work through a client problem with the interviewer, and the Personal Experience Interview, where one past experience is explored in depth with many follow-ups. Many candidates are first invited to Solve, McKinsey's online problem-solving game, and candidates commonly describe the cases as led by the interviewer, with maths and charts along the way.
rounds: First round: case interviews with a personal experience interview
Final round: more case and personal experience interviews

questions.text: Tell me about a time you persuaded someone who disagreed with you.
covers: Who they were, what they believed, and why their view made sense to them
What you did and said at each step, including what you changed after their pushback
The result, and how the relationship stood afterwards

questions.text: Our client's profits fell 15% this year. How would you work out why?
covers: A short structure first: revenue (price, volume, mix) and costs (fixed, variable)
Comparing with competitors and past years to see if it's the market or the client
A hypothesis, the data you'd ask for to test it, and a summary with next steps

questions.text: Tell me about a time you led a team through a difficult situation.
covers: What made it difficult and what was at stake for the team
The specific things you did as the leader, not what 'we' did
The outcome, and what you'd do differently next time

questions.text: Tell me about a time you set yourself an ambitious goal and kept going when it got hard.
covers: Why the goal was ambitious for you at the time
The obstacles and how you got past each one yourself
What you achieved, with a number or clear outcome

questions.text: Tell me about a time you brought together people with different views and made sure everyone was heard.
covers: Who was involved and why some voices were being missed
What you did to draw them in and use their ideas
How the result was better because of it

questions.text: Tell me about a time you pushed for a change that others were comfortable without.
covers: Why the change was needed and what the resistance was
The risk you took personally in pushing for it
How you won people over, and what changed as a result

questions.text: A regional airline is thinking about starting flights to a new country. How would you decide whether it should?
covers: The airline's goal and what success means: profit, growth or network strength
Market size and demand, competitors on the route, costs and the airline's own capabilities
A recommendation with the key risk and what you'd check before committing

questions.text: How would you estimate the number of fuel stations needed in Bengaluru? Talk me through your numbers.
covers: Starting from vehicles and how often each needs fuel
How many vehicles one station can serve in a day, with rounded assumptions
A final number and a quick check against what you'd expect to see

questions.text: A hospital wants to cut waiting times in its emergency department. How would you structure the problem?
covers: Following the patient's journey: arrival, triage, tests, treatment and discharge or admission
Finding the bottleneck with data: where patients wait longest and at what times
Practical fixes for the biggest bottleneck and how you'd measure the effect

questions.text: Your client's revenue is growing, but its market share is falling. What does that tell you, and what would you look at next?
covers: That the market is growing faster than the client
Which segments, regions or channels competitors are winning, and why
Whether this matters for the client's goals, and what to do about it

questions.text: If a store's costs are 80% of its revenue, and revenue rises 8% while costs rise 12%, what happens to its profit margin? Talk me through it.
covers: Setting revenue at 100: costs go from 80 to about 90 and revenue to 108
Profit falls from 20 to about 18, so the margin drops from 20% to about 17%
What that means for the client in one sentence

questions.text: A consumer goods company is deciding whether to buy a smaller rival. What would you want to know before recommending it?
covers: Why it wants the deal: growth, new products, customers or cost savings
The target's market, profitability and fit, and realistic savings from combining
Price versus value, the main risks, and a clear yes or no with conditions

questions.text: How would you explain to a client's chief executive what a machine-learning model can and can't do for their pricing?
covers: In plain words: it finds patterns in past sales to suggest prices
What it needs: clean data, enough history, and people who check its suggestions
Its limits: new situations, bias in past data, and how you'd test it safely first

questions.text: Why McKinsey, and why consulting rather than a role in industry?
covers: What you want from consulting: variety of problems, learning speed, impact on clients
Something specific about McKinsey you've learnt from its people or work
How it fits where you want to be in a few years

questions.text: Which industry or kind of problem would you most like to work on here, and why?
covers: A specific choice, not 'anything'
Why it interests you, shown by something you've read, studied or done
What you'd bring to that work

tips: Structure every case answer out loud before you solve it.
Prepare one deep story per personal experience theme; they'll probe it for 10–15 minutes.
Do case maths out loud with round numbers, say the units, and sanity-check the answer against the real world.
End each case with a clear recommendation, the main risk and what you'd check next, even if you haven't covered everything.
In the personal experience interview, choose stories where you personally made the difference; expect questions on what you thought, said and did at each step.
Practise with a partner who changes the facts mid-case, so a new question or chart doesn't throw you.
